idea: Johannes Blaeu-style 17th-century map of California drawn as an island, cartouche reading 'Confidently wrong for 150 years.' Wearable proof that a bad idea with a gorgeous engraving survives much longer than a true one.

Engraved 16th-century mariner's astrolabe from a navigation manual, with the caption 'Latitude: easy. Longitude: ask again in 1761.' For people who love the story of the longitude problem and the instrument that nearly solved it.

A Mercator-era globe gore (the flat lens-shaped printed segments of an early globe) laid out like a peeled orange, captioned 'The world, before assembly.' The gore engraving is beautiful and the joke is that every globe is a flat-pack reality.

The Mountains of Kong, an invented African mountain range copied onto maps for most of the 19th century, drawn as an engraved ridge line with the caption 'Copied by everyone. Seen by no one.' A shirt about how confidently errors get cited.

A 16th-century travel-book woodcut of a sea monster off a coast, with a small hand-lettered label pointing at it: 'Probably a whale. Definitely a deadline.' Old cartographers' monsters reframed as honest notes about uncertainty.

An 18th-century ship's hull lines plan (body plan, sheer and half-breadths from a naval architecture archive) with the caption 'Designed to be wrong in one direction only: forward.' Beautiful curves for people who love engineering drawings.

An engraved mariner's compass rose with all 32 points, where the north point is replaced by the word 'Somewhere' and the caption reads 'Wherever you meant to be, it is still a good rose.' Archive rose, one clean twist.
A 17th-century Dutch coastal sounding chart, rows of tiny depth numbers off a harbour, captioned 'Shallower than it looks.' Deadpan, for sailors and for anyone who has ever trusted a calm surface.

A field sketch of an explorer's camp from a 19th-century expedition narrative, with a caption in typewriter type: 'Day 41. Morale: surveyed.' Handwriting-scale diary fragment on a real engraving, funny to the right reader.

An engraved 18th-century sextant or octant from an instrument catalogue, captioned 'Measures the angle between where you are and where you thought you were.' Precision instruments as quiet philosophy.

Hereford-style medieval map fragment of the monstrous races (a sciapod using his single huge foot as a parasol), captioned 'Has an umbrella. Is the umbrella.' A beloved oddity from travel-book woodcuts, one-ink perfect.
Lewis and Clark-era hand-drawn river map sketch, or any explorer's river sketch, with the caption 'No one is lost. The river is just taking a longer route.' Warm and wry for hikers and wanderers.

The legendary island of Hy-Brasil, a perfect little circle cut by a cross that appears on maps off Ireland from 1325 to the 1800s, captioned 'Appeared on maps for 500 years. Declined to appear on land.' For lovers of phantom islands.

An engraved cross-staff or backstaff used to sight the sun, drawn large, with the caption 'Do not look directly at the problem.' Wry safety advice borrowed from a navigator who always stood with his back to the sun.

A 16th-century portolan-style coastline of the Mediterranean with hundreds of port names radiating inland, re-captioned 'Everything important happens at the edge.' Lovely line density, and an actual point of view.
A polar explorer's sledge from a 19th-century Arctic expedition engraving, captioned 'Packed for every outcome except this one.' Gentle humour for people who plan too much.

Early world map with the unknown southern continent Terra Australis Incognita engraved as a huge blank landmass, captioned 'Terra Incognita. Currently accepting rumours.' The mapmakers' confidence, one line of text.

A 17th-century engraving of a cartographer's dividers and a pair of compasses crossed over a tiny coastline, captioned 'Measure twice. Name once. Be blamed forever.' For anyone whose name ended up on something by accident.
The Piri Reis-style coastline with a drawn border of tiny sailing ships, where one ship is circled by hand and labelled 'You are here (probably).' Funny in the way real navigation always is.

A 1700s star chart of the southern sky engraved with Lacaille's invented constellations (Air Pump, Microscope, Sculptor's Workshop), captioned 'He named 14 constellations after lab equipment.' For the geeks who found this out and loved it.
